title: Codespaces, dev containers and AI coding agents
summary: A dev container describes a working environment in a file, a codespace runs it in the cloud, and a coding agent can work inside one on a branch of its own. The environment becomes reproducible, and the agent becomes a contributor whose pull requests you review.
outcomes: Write a `devcontainer.json` that gives every contributor the same Python environment
Choose between github.dev, a codespace and a local dev container for a task
Stop, resume and delete codespaces without losing work
Delegate a scoped task to a coding agent and review what comes back
Apply least privilege and confidentiality rules when AI tools touch your code

lenses.everyday: A rented vacation kitchen comes fully stocked: the same pans, the same knives, the same oven the listing promised. You cook, you leave, and the next guest gets an identical kitchen. That is a codespace built from a dev container file. A coding agent is a capable temp to whom you hand a clearly written task and a spare kitchen. They cook the dish and put it on the counter for you to taste. You decide whether it goes to the table. The temp never serves guests directly.
lenses.legal: A firm issues each new associate a standard laptop image, so nobody loses a week to setup and every machine meets policy. A dev container is that standard image, defined in a file under version control. A coding agent is closer to a contract attorney on a discrete assignment: a written scope, access limited to the matter, work product delivered as a draft, and a supervising attorney who reviews and signs. The duty of supervision does not transfer. Neither do confidentiality obligations: before client or employer material goes to an outside service, the engagement terms and firm policy have to allow it.
lenses.ml: A new collaborator joins on Monday. Without a dev container they spend the day matching your Python version, system libraries and Jupyter extensions, and still end up with a different NumPy. With one, they press a button and get the environment the tests ran in. Then you hand a coding agent a task: add a `--seed` flag to `train.py`, thread it through the data loader, and add a test. It works in its own environment on a branch and opens a pull request. CI runs. You read the diff like any other, because your name is on the merge.
lenses.technical: A dev container is a container-based environment described by `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`: a base image, optional features, forwarded ports, editor extensions and commands to run after creation. GitHub Codespaces builds that container on a cloud virtual machine and connects an editor to it. github.dev is a browser editor with no compute and no terminal. A coding agent is an AI system that takes a task, runs tools in an isolated environment, commits to a branch and opens a pull request. Rulesets, required checks and review apply to its pull requests exactly as they do to a person's.

sections.heading: Three places to edit, and when to use each

items.title: github.dev
points: Press {{.}} on any repository page
An editor in the browser, open in a second
No terminal, and no running code
Good for edits across several files and for reading code with search

items.title: Codespace
points: A full machine in the cloud, with a terminal
Built from the repository's dev container
Runs tests, notebooks and servers
Metered, and stops when idle

items.title: Local dev container
points: The same container, on your own computer
Needs Docker and VS Code's Dev Containers extension
Works offline and uses your hardware
No cloud usage to pay for

blocks.text: All three give you the VS Code interface. The difference is what sits behind it: nothing, a cloud machine, or your own machine.

blocks.prompt: You open a repository in github.dev, edit `train.py`, and want to run the tests before committing. Can you?
blocks.answer: No. github.dev has no terminal and no compute, so nothing can run. You can commit and let CI test the change, or continue in a codespace, which has both. github.dev is for editing. A codespace is for editing and running.

blocks.text: The file lives at `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`. Commit it, and every codespace and every local dev container starts from the same definition.

head: Key
What it does
rows: The base container image. This one has Python 3.12 and common tools
Prebuilt add-ons, each installing one tool. Here, the `gh` command
Runs once after the container is created. Install your dependencies here
Ports to make reachable from your browser, such as 8888 for Jupyter
Editor extensions and settings to preinstall

blocks.title: Pin what matters
blocks.text: A tag such as `python:3.12` moves as patch versions are released. That is usually what you want for development. For an environment that must reproduce a published result, pin the image by digest and install from a lock file. [Reproducible research repositories](#advanced-research-repro) covers this.

items: **Work is not on GitHub until you push.** A codespace has its own disk. Commit and push before you stop for the day.
**Idle codespaces stop on their own** after a timeout, and stopped ones are deleted after a longer period without use. Both periods are adjustable in your settings.
**Stopped is not free.** A stopped codespace uses no compute but still occupies storage.
**One codespace per task works well.** Create it from the branch or pull request, do the work, push, delete it.
**Codespaces secrets are their own store.** Add them in your personal settings or the repository's Codespaces secrets, and they appear as environment variables.
**It is a development machine.** Use it to write, test and run small experiments. Long training jobs belong on infrastructure built for them.

blocks.title: Usage is metered
blocks.text: Codespaces usage is measured in compute time and storage, with an included amount that depends on your account. Your billing settings show current usage, and you can set a budget there if you want a hard stop.

sections.heading: AI in the loop: assistants and agents

items.title: In-editor assistant
points: Suggests code as you type and answers questions about open files
You accept or reject each suggestion
Works at the speed of your attention
You are the author of every change

items.title: Coding agent
points: Takes a whole task and works on its own
Runs commands, edits files and reacts to test failures
Delivers a branch and a pull request
You are the reviewer, and the person who merges

blocks.text: GitHub Copilot coding agent and Claude Code are two examples of the second kind, and there are others. They differ in where they run and how you start them: from an issue, a chat, a terminal or a phone. What they share matters more. The work arrives as commits on a branch, and the pull request is the checkpoint where a person decides.

steps.label: CI runs
steps.note: The same required checks as anyone

blocks.caption: An agent's work passes through the same gates as a person's

blocks.code:
## Outcome
`scripts/train.py` accepts `--seed` and produces identical metrics for two runs with the same seed.

## In scope
- `scripts/train.py`
- `src/project/data.py` (shuffling only)
- a new test in `tests/test_seed.py`

## Out of scope
- Model code, configs, and anything under `.github/`
- New dependencies

## How I will check it
- `python -m pytest tests/test_seed.py` passes
- The diff touches only the files listed above
blocks.caption: A task written so that an agent, or a person, cannot misread its edges

items: **Write the task like a good issue.** State the outcome, the files in scope, what must not change, and how you will check it.
**Keep it small.** A task you could review in fifteen minutes is the right size. Large tasks produce large diffs that nobody reads properly.
**Branch and pull request, always.** Your rulesets already require this. The agent should meet the same guardrails as a person.
**Read the diff, not the summary.** The agent's description says what it intended. The diff says what it did.
**Look for the quiet shortcuts**: a deleted or skipped test, a loosened assertion, a broad exception handler, a new dependency, a changed workflow file.
**Let CI vote.** Required checks apply. If the agent's workflow runs wait for your approval to start, read any workflow changes before approving.
**Give it the least access that works.** A token for one repository, no deployment secrets, and no ability to approve or merge its own work.

blocks.text: Most tools read a repository instruction file where you record conventions once: how to run the tests, the style rules, what never to touch. The file name differs by tool. Examples are `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. Check your tool's documentation for the name it reads, and review that file like code, because it steers every future task.

blocks.title: Confidentiality comes first
blocks.text: Before you send code to any AI service, check what your employer's or client's policy allows and what the service does with what it receives. Source code can be a trade secret, can include personal data, and can be covered by a confidentiality agreement you signed. Ownership and licensing of generated code are separate questions with unsettled edges. This is general information, not legal advice. For the wider picture see [The non-code layer](#expert-law-tax-access).

blocks.title: Accountability does not delegate
blocks.text: A merged pull request is yours, whoever or whatever wrote it. If you would not approve the change from a new colleague without reading it, do not approve it from an agent.

blocks.title: Agents as an accommodation
blocks.text: Delegating typing-heavy or sequencing-heavy work can be a real accommodation for people with repetitive strain injuries, limited energy or a heavy executive-function load. The review step is what keeps it safe. Tools that let you start a task by voice or from a phone, and review later on your own schedule, widen who can contribute.

howto.task: Create a codespace and work in it
browser: On the repository page select **Code**, open the **Codespaces** tab, and select **Create codespace on main**.
Wait for the editor to load. The terminal at the bottom is a shell inside the container.
Create a branch, edit, and run your tests in the terminal.
Commit and push from the Source Control view.
When you are done, stop the codespace from the same **Codespaces** tab or at github.com/codespaces, and delete it once your work is pushed.
phone: GitHub Mobile does not run codespaces as of this writing.
A codespace opens in a mobile browser from github.com/codespaces. The editor works, though a small screen and an on-screen keyboard make it slow.
That is good enough for a small fix, running one command, or checking a result. For longer work a tablet with a keyboard is the practical minimum.
From the same page you can stop or delete codespaces, a useful phone task when you remember one is still running.
cli: `gh codespace create` and choose the repository, branch and machine size.
`gh codespace list` to see what you have and whether each is running.
`gh codespace ssh` to open a shell in one, or `gh codespace code` to open it in VS Code.
`gh codespace stop` when you pause, and `gh codespace delete` after your work is pushed.
editor: Install the GitHub Codespaces extension in VS Code and sign in.
Open the Command Palette and run **Codespaces: Create New Codespace**, or connect to an existing one.
You now have your desktop editor in front and the cloud machine behind it.
To use the same definition locally, install the Dev Containers extension and run **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**. Docker must be running.
A coding agent started in the codespace's terminal inherits that environment, including its repository-scoped token.

howto.task: Delegate a task to a coding agent and review the result
browser: Write the task as an issue: outcome, files in scope, what not to change, how to verify.
Start the agent the way your tool provides, for example by assigning the issue to it or starting a session from its web interface.
When the pull request appears, open **Files changed** and read every file. Tick **Viewed** on each file to track your progress.
Check the workflow results. If runs are waiting for approval, read any workflow changes before you approve them.
Request changes in review comments as you would for a person. Merge only when you would sign your name to it.
phone: Some agents can be started from their own mobile app or a web page, which makes a phone a reasonable place to hand off a well-written task.
Review in GitHub Mobile: open the pull request, read the changed files, and check the status of the checks.
Small, clearly scoped diffs can be reviewed and merged from the app. Leave large or security-sensitive diffs for a bigger screen. Reviewing carefully matters more than reviewing now.
cli: Create a branch for the agent's work, or let the agent create one. Confirm with `git branch --show-current` that it is not `main`.
Run the agent in the repository folder and give it the scoped task.
`git diff main...HEAD` to read everything it changed, and `git log --oneline main..HEAD` to see its commits.
Run the tests yourself. Do not rely on the agent's report that they pass.
`gh pr diff` and `gh pr view --comments` for a final read before merging.
editor: Start the task from the assistant or agent panel in your editor, with the relevant files open for context.
Review the changes in the Source Control view's diff, one file at a time, before staging anything.
Stage only what you have read. Discard what you do not want.
Commit with a message that describes the change in your own words, push, and open a pull request with the GitHub Pull Requests extension.
Record standing conventions in the repository's instruction file, so you do not repeat them in every prompt.

pitfalls.trap: Leaving work uncommitted in a codespace that is later deleted for inactivity.
pitfalls.fix: Push before you stop. Treat the codespace as disposable and the remote branch as the only safe place.

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting running or stopped codespaces and being surprised by the usage.
pitfalls.fix: Look at github.com/codespaces weekly, delete what is finished, and shorten the idle timeout in settings.

pitfalls.trap: Approving an agent's pull request because the description sounds right and the checks pass.
pitfalls.fix: Read the diff. Look specifically for removed or weakened tests and for changes outside the stated scope.

pitfalls.trap: Pasting a secret or a confidential document into an AI chat to give it context.
pitfalls.fix: Never paste credentials. For confidential material, confirm policy first, and prefer describing the shape of the data over sharing the data.

pitfalls.trap: Letting an agent run with your full personal token and write access to everything.
pitfalls.fix: Use a fine-grained token for one repository, and keep deployment secrets in environments the agent cannot reach.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between github.dev and a codespace?
choices: github.dev is paid and codespaces are free
A codespace has a terminal and compute; github.dev is an editor only
github.dev works only on public repositories
They are two names for the same thing
quiz.why: github.dev runs entirely in your browser with nothing behind it, so it can edit and commit but not execute. A codespace is a cloud machine, so it can run tests, notebooks and servers.

quiz.q: Where does the definition of a repository's development environment live?
choices: In each developer's personal settings
In `.github/workflows/`
In `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`, committed to the repository
In the repository's About section
quiz.why: The dev container file is version-controlled with the code. The environment changes through reviewed pull requests, and everyone, in a codespace or a local container, builds from the same definition.

quiz.q: You stop a codespace with uncommitted changes and return three days later. What is the state of your work?
choices: Still there, as long as the codespace has not been deleted
Lost, because stopping discards the disk
Automatically pushed to a backup branch
Committed to `main`
quiz.why: Stopping keeps the disk. The risk is deletion, either after a long period without use or by your own hand. Nothing is pushed automatically, which is why you push before you stop.

quiz.q: An agent's pull request has passing checks and a clear description. Which review step is still essential?
choices: None; passing checks are sufficient
Re-running CI twice to be sure
Asking the agent whether it is confident
Reading the diff for changes outside the scope and for tests that were removed or weakened
quiz.why: Checks only prove that the tests which exist still pass. An agent can reach a passing result by changing the tests. The diff is the only complete record of what changed, and the person who merges is accountable for it.

quiz.q: Which access setup best fits a coding agent working on one repository?
choices: Your classic token with every scope
A fine-grained token for that repository, with no deployment secrets and no ability to merge
Organization owner rights, so it never gets blocked
No authentication at all
quiz.why: Least privilege limits the damage from a mistake or a manipulated instruction. The agent needs to push a branch and open a pull request. It does not need production secrets or the power to approve its own work.

mission.title: Give your repository a dev container and delegate one task
mission.where: Your own repository. The agent step is optional and works with whichever tool you already use.
steps: Add `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` from this lesson on a branch, adjusted to your Python version and requirements file. Merge it by pull request.
Create a codespace from `main`. In its terminal run `python --version` and your tests, and confirm the environment matches the file.
Make a small change on a branch inside the codespace, push it, then stop and delete the codespace.
Press {{.}} on the repository page to open github.dev. Note what is missing compared with the codespace.
Write a fifteen-minute task as an issue with an outcome, a scope, exclusions and a verification step.
If you use a coding agent, hand it the issue. Review its pull request against the supervision list in this lesson, and write one review comment before deciding.
Open github.com/codespaces and confirm nothing is left running.

terms.def: A development environment defined by a file in the repository and run as a container, so every contributor gets the same tools.
The configuration file, usually in `.devcontainer/`, that names the image, features, extensions and setup commands for a dev container.
A cloud-hosted development machine built from a repository's dev container, with an editor and a terminal.
A browser-based editor for any repository, opened by pressing the period key. It has no terminal and runs no code.
A prepackaged add-on that installs one tool or runtime into a dev container image.
An AI system that carries out a development task on its own: editing files, running commands and opening a pull request for review.
A file in the repository that tells AI tools the project's conventions. Its name depends on the tool.
A design where a person reviews and approves automated work before it takes effect. The pull request is that checkpoint.

commands.does: Creates a codespace for a repository and branch you choose.
Lists your codespaces and whether each is running or stopped.
Opens a terminal session inside a codespace.
Stops a running codespace. Its disk is kept.
Deletes a codespace and its disk. Unpushed work in it is lost.
On a repository or pull request page, opens it in the github.dev editor.
Shows everything the current branch changed since it left `main`. The first thing to read after an agent finishes.
Prints the full diff of the current branch's pull request in the terminal.
